extracted.intended_audience: researchers, research administrators, and funding agency staff involved in faculty recruitment and peer review
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and empirical analysis of how external peer-review merit scores relate to an objective composite bibliometric track-record for applicants to Assistant Professor and Senior Researcher positions, with recommendations to reduce bias in recruitment/review. Focus is on assessing and improving faculty recruitment peer review and metric-based merit assessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: External reviewer merit score (0–7 scale)
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicants are graded between 0 and 7 for merits, where 7 = Exceptional, 6 = Excellent, 5 = Very good to Excellent, 4 = Very Good, 3 = Good, 2 = Weak, 1 = Poor, 0 = Insufficient information provided for assessment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Merit scores analyzed in this study are based on (1) publications and (2) academic education and research merits. Publications include published papers and scientific presentations. Academic education and research merits includes education, experience of research, competence, independence, research network, financing, prizes, and invitations to present or review. Six external reviewers (professors at other Swedish universities, with equal gender distribution) provide one score for merits (based on the CV) and one for the project plan and return a ranking to KI.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composite bibliometric score (0–7)
rubrics_metrics.description: A computed track-record metric summing seven standardized bibliometric variables to quantify applicant productivity; each part is log-transformed and normalized within the applicant pool so the smallest value = 0 and largest = 1, yielding a composite score between 0 and 7.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Score adapted from previous work (Holst and Hägg 2018) and inspired by Wennerås and Wold (1997). Calculated only on applicants selected for external review; when pooling across years, only first application instance per person was included. Intended as an objective proxy for productivity that can be used to compare with subjective reviewer scores and as quality control for bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Number of publications
rubrics_metrics.description: Component #1 of the composite bibliometric score representing raw output (the number of publications).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publications considered are articles and reviews available in Web of Science from 1995 to time of application. Librarians manually verified publications using PMIDs and cross-checked journal, title, and author position when PMIDs were incorrectly input.

rubrics_metrics.name: Total number of citations
rubrics_metrics.description: Component #2 of the composite bibliometric score representing impact (total citations to the applicant's publications).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Citations were retrieved from Web of Science (Clarivate). This component is log-transformed and normalized within the applicant pool before summation into the composite score.

rubrics_metrics.name: Share of publications as first author
rubrics_metrics.description: Component #3 of the composite bibliometric score representing ability to lead a project at a junior level (proportion of publications where the applicant was first author).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to infer junior leadership potential; part of the seven-part composite metric, log-transformed and normalized among selected applicants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Share of publications as last author
rubrics_metrics.description: Component #4 of the composite bibliometric score representing ability to lead a project at a senior level (proportion of publications where the applicant was last author).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to infer senior leadership/PI-level contributions; included as one standardized component in the composite score.

rubrics_metrics.name: H-index
rubrics_metrics.description: Component #5 of the composite bibliometric score representing consistency of impact across publications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: H-index computed from Web of Science data, log-transformed and normalized within the applicant pool for inclusion in the composite score.

rubrics_metrics.name: Share of publications in high-impact journals within field (field-normalization metric)
rubrics_metrics.description: Component #6: proportion of publications in high-impact journals within the publication's field to represent perceived quality and visibility in field context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Field defined using Clarivate's journal categorization. Within a field, the top two journals by Journal Impact Factor are considered high impact. This component is intended as a field-normalized metric of visibility/likely impact; it is log-transformed and normalized prior to summation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Binary indicator for any publication in a high-impact journal overall
rubrics_metrics.description: Component #7: a binary bonus indicating whether the applicant has any publication in a high-impact journal overall.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Overall 'high impact' journals defined as the top 30 journals by Journal Impact Factor. Presence/absence is coded and incorporated as one standardized component of the composite score.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manual verification of publications
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure publication lists provided by applicants accurately reflect authorship and author position via librarian verification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: KI librarians manually verified all published articles using the PMID reported in the application; if the PMID was incorrect, librarians searched the journal, article title, and author. If an author's name was missing from metadata, the full text was checked for the name. This verification underpins the accuracy of bibliometric components.

rubrics_metrics.name: Field-normalization method for high-impact identification
rubrics_metrics.description: Define 'field' using Clarivate journal categories and label high-impact journals within field as the top two by JIF, with an overall top-30 list for cross-field high-impact designation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journal Impact Factors were obtained from Journal Citation Reports (Clarivate). This operational definition is used to compute components #6 and #7 of the composite score and to attempt field-normalized assessment of visibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Z-normalization and assessor-scale checking
rubrics_metrics.description: Test whether different reviewers use different grading scales and apply Z-normalization to compensate if needed: Z = (X – M)/S.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intraclass correlation coefficients (ICCs) were computed before and after standardization; if ICCs show sufficient homogeneity (as in 2014–2016) normalization may be unnecessary. In this study, analyses were performed on non-normalized data because ICCs were sufficiently high in 2014–2016 and normalization was not deemed necessary from 2017 onward.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer composition and number for external assessment
rubrics_metrics.description: External review step involved six external reviewers (professors at other Swedish universities) with equal gender distribution, scoring each application on merits and project plan.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Six reviewers each provide merit and project scores and return a ranking to KI. The study cites literature suggesting low agreement among reviewers and references a preprint estimating that many more reviewers (e.g., 12) may be needed for reliable evaluations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blinded assessment of project proposals (semi-blinded three-step process)
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposal to reduce bias by having project plans reviewed blinded to applicant identity (especially when applicants are junior).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Figure 4 and Discussion propose a three-step process: (1) blinded review of project plans, (2) computation of a composite bibliometric score to quantify past productivity, and (3) an individual reviewer integrates the blinded project assessment and the bibliometric score into an overall assessment; intended to reduce bias while allowing assessment of innovativeness and competency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use computed track record as quality control
rubrics_metrics.description: Grants/appointments bodies should compute applicants' track records (e.g., composite bibliometric score) and use them to assess whether bias affects reviewer assessments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare computed productivity with subjective reviewer merit scores to detect differential treatment by gender; institutions should self-assess whether merit/competence scores correlate with productivity and whether scoring is well matched across demographic groups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correct bibliometric metrics for known biases
rubrics_metrics.description: When using bibliometric measures, adjust or correct for known citation and field biases (e.g., a field-specific 'bias factor').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Composite bibliometry itself can be biased (e.g., citation gender bias); future optimization of the composite score should aim to ensure in-built citation bias does not compound existing bias. A field-specific correction factor is proposed as one mitigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anonymization thresholds for reporting field-term networks
rubrics_metrics.description: Protect individual integrity when reporting field-level analyses (MeSH networks) by only showing nodes/terms that meet minimum counts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To maintain anonymization, for a MeSH term (node) to show in network figures at least two Assistant Professor applicants or three Senior Researcher applicants had to have the same term; data presented at group level to preclude identification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional self-assessment and standardization of evaluation templates
rubrics_metrics.description: Standardize templates and assessment frameworks across agencies/institutions to reduce variability and potential bias in reviewer evaluation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites Finland's program to establish a standardized template across funding bodies and recommends that granting bodies adopt standardized evaluation templates and conduct regular quality control (e.g., testing correlations between objective productivity measures and reviewer scores).

rubrics_metrics.name: Statistical approach for detecting bias in scoring
rubrics_metrics.description: Use linear regression of objective productivity (composite bibliometric score) against external reviewer scores, including gender and interaction terms, to detect differential slopes/intercepts by gender.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretation: slope tests whether reviewer scores increase with productivity; gender term tests overall difference in scores between men and women; interaction term tests whether the relationship (slope) differs by gender. Use R, report R, R-square, F, df, and consider p < 0.05 significant. Remove repeat applicants when pooling by using only first application instance.
